'''Ryan''' "'''Skip'''" '''Garibaldi''' is an American mathematician doing research on [[Lottery mathematics|lotteries]] and [[algebraic group]]s, especially [[exceptional groups]].

==Biography==

Garibaldi dropped out of high school to attend [[Purdue University]], where he earned [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] degrees in mathematics and in computer science.<ref name="lottery">{{cite web | url = http://mathdl.maa.org/mathDL/22/?pa=content&sa=viewDocument&nodeId=3728 | title = Finding Good Bets in the Lottery, and Why You Shouldn't Take Them | publisher = Mathematical Association of America | year = 2010 | last1 = Abrams | first1 = Aaron | last2 = Garibaldi | first2 = Skip | access-date = 16 September 2011}} (article from 2010, reprinted on MAA website in 2011 due to award)</ref>  He then obtained a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in mathematics from the [[University of California, San Diego]] in 1998.  His doctoral thesis was on [[triality]] and algebraic groups.  After holding positions at [[ETH Zurich]] and the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], (with Jared Hersh serving as his long-time Reader and typist) he joined the faculty at [[Emory University]] in 2002, and was eventually promoted to Winship Distinguished Research Professor.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.alumni.emory.edu/events-and-programs/faculty-within-your-reach/bio-garibaldi.html | title = Skip Garibaldi: Winship Distinguished Professor of Mathematics and Science | publisher = Emory University Alumni Association | access-date = 16 September 2011}}</ref>  In 2013 he became associate director of [[Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics|IPAM]] at [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]].<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.ipam.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/IPAM-Newsletter-2013-FINAL.pdf | title = IPAM Newsletter Fall 2013 | publisher = [[Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics]] | access-date = 2 June 2015}}</ref> As of 2026, he was vice president and director of the [[Institute for Defense Analyses]] Center for Communications Research, La Jolla.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ryan "Skip" Garibaldi, Ph.D. |url=https://www.ida.org/about-ida/leadership/ryan-garibaldi-ph-d |access-date=2026-08-06 |website=IDA |language=en}}</ref>

===On lottery mathematics===
{{see also|Lottery mathematics}}
Garibaldi plays the lottery and has shared some math-based tips to increase the chances of winning the jackpot solo, rather than winning per se. He advises against betting on the same numbers as well as [[Sequence number|sequential numbers]] (as lotto jackpot winner [[Richard Lustig]] advocated) in favor of "unpopular numbers", i.e., randomly generated numbers which do not represent anything nor that other bettors would pick. He explains that the latter strategy decreases the odds of splitting the jackpot whereas the former strategies increase it.<ref>{{cite magazine | url = https://www.wired.com/video/watch/lottery-strategy | title = Mathematician Breaks Down the Best Ways to Win the Lottery | magazine = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] | date = April 4, 2023 | access-date = June 27, 2023}}</ref>

Garibaldi has written less-technical articles on the lottery<ref name="lottery"/><ref name="lottery2">{{cite journal |last1=Arratia |first1=Richard|author-link=Richard Arratia|last2=Garibaldi|first2=Skip|last3=Mower|first3=Lawrence|last4=Stark|first4=Philip |arxiv=1503.02902 |title=Some people have all the luck |doi=10.4169/math.mag.88.3.196 |volume=88 |issue=3 |journal=Mathematics Magazine |year=2015|pages=196–211|s2cid=15631424}}</ref> which led to TV appearances and policy changes in Florida<ref>{{cite news |last=Mower |first=Lawrence |date=2 April 2014 |title=Florida lottery announces changes in response to The Post's investigation on repeat winners |url=http://www.mypalmbeachpost.com/news/news/state-regional/lottery-announces-changes-in-response-to-post-inve/nfQK7/ |newspaper=[[The Palm Beach Post]] |location=Palm Beach, Florida|access-date=2 June 2015}}</ref> and Georgia.<ref>{{cite news |last=Sposito |first=Sean |date=18 September 2014 |title=Lottery lets players collect 100-plus prizes. Is something fishy?|url=http://www.myajc.com/news/news/state-regional-govt-politics/lottery-overlooked-highly-improbable-win-patterns/nhPr8/|newspaper=[[The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]] |location=Atlanta, Georgia|access-date=2 June 2015}}</ref>  

==Scientific contributions==

Garibaldi's most-cited work is the book "Cohomological invariants in Galois cohomology"<ref>{{cite book| last = Garibaldi | first = Skip |author2=Alexander Merkurjev |author3=Jean-Pierre Serre|title=Cohomological invariants in Galois cohomology | publisher = [[American Mathematical Society]]|year = 2003|series=University Lecture Series 28|isbn= 0-8218-3287-5}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Swallow, John|title=Review: ''Cohomological invariants in Galois cohomology'', by Skip Garibaldi, Alexander Merkurjev, and Jean-Pierre Serre|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.)|year=2004|volume=42|issue=1|pages=93–98|url=http://www.ams.org/journals/bull/2005-42-01/S0273-0979-04-01033-X/S0273-0979-04-01033-X.pdf|doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-04-01033-X|doi-access=free}}</ref> written with [[Alexander Merkurjev]] and [[Jean-Pierre Serre]], which gives the foundations of the theory of cohomological invariants of algebraic groups.  His long work "Cohomological invariants: exceptional groups and Spin groups"<ref>{{cite book| last = Garibaldi | first = Skip|title=Cohomological invariants: exceptional groups and Spin groups | publisher = [[American Mathematical Society]]|year = 2009|series=[[Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society]]|isbn= 978-0-8218-4404-5}}</ref> built on this theme.

He received press coverage<ref>{{cite web | url = https://arstechnica.com/science/news/2010/03/setting-the-record-straight-no-simple-theory-of-everything.ars | title = Setting the record straight: no simple theory of everything | publisher = [[Ars Technica]] | year = 2010 | last1 = Ford | first1 = Matt | access-date = 17 September 2011}}
</ref> for his paper "There is no Theory of Everything inside E<sub>8</sub>"<ref name="DistlerGaribaldi">{{cite journal |author1=Jacques Distler |author2=Skip Garibaldi |title=There is no "Theory of Everything" inside E8 |doi=10.1007/s00220-010-1006-y |year=2010 |journal=[[Communications in Mathematical Physics]] |volume=298 |issue=2 |pages=419–436 |arxiv=0905.2658 |bibcode=2010CMaPh.298..419D|s2cid=15074118 }}</ref> with [[Jacques Distler]] proposing a disproof of [[Garrett Lisi]]'s "[[An Exceptionally Simple Theory of Everything]]".

He contributed to a story in [[Slate (magazine)|Slate magazine]] by Chris Wilson<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.slate.com/id/2256250/ | title = 13 Stripes and 51 Stars | publisher = Slate | year = 2010 | last1 = Wilson | first1 = Chris | access-date = 17 September 2011}}
</ref> about arranging stars on the [[Flag of the United States|US flag]] that was reported on [[CBS News Sunday Morning]].

==Recognition==
In 2011 he received the [[Lester R. Ford Award]] from the [[Mathematical Association of America]].<ref name="lottery"/>

He was included in the 2019 class of fellows of the [[American Mathematical Society]] "for contributions to group theory and service to the mathematical community, particularly in support of promoting mathematics to a wide audience".<ref>{{citation|url=https://www.ams.org/profession/ams-fellows/new-fellows|title=2019 Class of the Fellows of the AMS|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|access-date=2018-11-07}}</ref>
